children: By Dave Michaels

It has been eight years since the Supreme Court effectively opened up the nation to sports betting, giving hundreds of millions of Americans the ability to gamble at home. With the rise of prediction markets, it will soon face the question of whether to upend the landscape again.

Kalshi has stormed into sports wagers, challenging top online sportsbooks including DraftKings and FanDuel. It has marketed aggressively through television ads featuring superstar athletes and celebrities, airing them during the recent U.S. Open and the kickoff of the NFL season.

Still, Kalshi and other prediction markets argue their wagers, offered as a type of financial contract and traded on an exchange, aren't gambling at all and therefore should be exempt from state supervision. That has prompted lawsuits from angry states, which collect billions of dollars in tax revenue from sports-betting platforms.

Dozens of lawsuits, which include complaints by tribal governments, are moving through state and federal courts. Kalshi has been on the losing end of many rulings, but secured a big appeals-court victory against the state of New Jersey, prompting state officials to seek Supreme Court review. Because another appeals court ruled against Kalshi, the justices may feel compelled to resolve the dispute in the coming months. And how the case plays out could have ramifications far beyond sports contests.
"We are just at the tip of the iceberg in terms of the legal questions about what is being offered on prediction markets," said John Holden, an Indiana University business law professor.

The downside for states is huge if Kalshi wins, since it could lead more gamblers to switch from sportsbooks that pay taxes on gaming revenue to prediction markets that largely don't. The gambling industry generated $17.9 billion last year in tax revenue for state and local governments.

In addition to sports, prediction markets offer traders yes-or-no bets on everything from which political party will control Congress to the Federal Reserve's next interest-rate decision to which words President Trump will use in a speech. Kalshi, the biggest U.S. prediction market, says they are swaps, a type of bet on a future event that Wall Street developed to address risk tied to interest rates, credit risk and currencies.
Participants on Kalshi's market bet against one another, not against a company that sets odds.

Kalshi is now the third-largest online sports betting platform after DraftKings and FanDuel, according to gaming research firm Eilers & Krejcik. About 70% of Kalshi's daily trading volume comes from sports betting, according to the prediction-market operator.
DraftKings, FanDuel and other copycats launched prediction markets after Kalshi and an early competitor, Polymarket, caught fire with betting on sports and politics.

Prediction markets are slightly more costly to use for a 50/50 bet than online sportsbooks, according to estimates from investment bank Jefferies, but they are popular with risk-seeking young traders and open to citizens in states including Texas and California where sports betting is prohibited. Thirty-nine states allow sports gambling in some form.

A Supreme Court decision that states can regulate prediction markets' sports contracts could crimp Kalshi's profits from those bets. State taxes on online sports betting range from 10% to 51% of gaming revenues. It also could lead to new challenges from states over other controversial bets, including ones based on federal and state elections.

"There are high stakes because this is such a novel market and has exponentially grown in such a significant way and in such a short period of time," said Kristin Johnson, a former member of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission who teaches at George Washington University Law School.

Much of the legal fight over prediction markets turns on whether their sports bets qualify as swaps, a type of financial derivative whose value depends on an event with a "potential financial, economic, or commercial consequence."
If so, then federal regulation would pre-empt state supervision, according to the CFTC and Kalshi.

The Trump administration backs Kalshi's ability to offer sports bets, with the CFTC filing nine lawsuits against states trying to regulate prediction markets. The CFTC oversees Kalshi and other prediction markets, with its Trump-appointed chairman arguing they foster valuable information.

Some state law enforcers and former regulators say the CFTC has let Kalshi stampede over the agency's core mission, which is ensuring fair and resilient trading in derivatives markets used by investors, farmers, ranchers and large businesses.
"Sports bets have nothing to do with that," said Tim Massad, a CFTC chairman during the Obama administration who has worked with states on prediction markets.

In the New Jersey case, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit ruled in April that Kalshi's bets are exempt from state gaming laws. Last month, a similar panel of judges sitting in San Francisco, found the opposite.

The West Coast panel pointed out that the CFTC has taken conflicting positions toward prediction markets. A rule promulgated in 2011 disallowed swaps tied to "gaming," which the agency says includes bets on sports.
The CFTC is now trying to change that rule before the cases get to the Supreme Court.

Kalshi's sports bets appear to fit within Congress's definition of swaps in a 2010 law prompted by the financial crisis two years earlier, said David Zaring, a business law professor at the University of Pennsylvania. But it makes little sense to think a law intended to bridle Wall Street also opened the gates to sports betting, Zaring said.

"There is no way Congress wanted sports gambling to be regulated by the CFTC exclusively," he said. "And there is no way that states would have signed up for a regime where they are pre-empted from regulating gambling."
